To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the rate of growth of oxycel crystals in aqueous suspension increases as the temperature of the suspension is increased, (ii) the rate of crystal growth in theophylline aqueous suspension increases with time, and (iii) the rate of oxycel crystal growth in suspension increases as the concentration of the suspension is decreased, whereas that of theophylline decreases.
the growth of oxycolzanide crystals in suspensions is due to a solvent‐mediated polymorphic transformation, whereas that of theophylline is due to hydration.
the growth of unsolvated crystals in aqueous suspensions is the result of a phase transition between two polymorphs and the growth of solvated crystals in aqueously‐based systems is due to hydration.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the growth of crystals from aqueous solutions of drugs and other materials.
the growth of crystals in aqueous drug systems and the effects of phase transitions on crystal size.
the application of physical methods to the elucidation of the mechanisms involved in the crystallization of drugs.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the rate‐controlling mechanism in both systems is a solid‐state process, i.e., a phase transition.
the growth of crystals from solution is not a simple phenomenon and that the mechanism is dependent upon the particular system.

the crystal growth process in aqueous drug solutions is a complicated function of the solute, the solvent, the solution composition, the solution temperature, the crystal size, and the crystal morphology.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the crystal growth of a number of drugs in aqueous suspensions is a result of a phase transition.
the growth of crystals in suspension is a complex phenomenon, which can be understood only by a detailed study of the phase transitions occurring within the system.
the growth of crystals in quiescentsuspensions of drugs may be due to either solvent‐mediated or water‐mediated phase transitions.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the growth of crystals in aqueous suspensions is a complex process involving several different mechanisms.
the growth of crystals in suspensions is not necessarily a result of the Ostwald ripening process, which has been the subject of much research.
the growth of oxycel crystals in quiescence is due to an isothermal, solvated‐mediated phase conversion.
